inputs.need:
I coordinate the 12-month nurse residency program for new graduate registered nurses at our 640-bed regional teaching hospital. We take three intakes a year (February, June and October) of about 70 new graduates each. Retention is our biggest worry: in the last three years between 19 and 26 percent of each intake left the hospital within 12 months of hire, and every nurse who leaves costs us months of orientation and preceptor time.

At the month-3 residency seminar every resident completes our Transition Check, a 15-item self-rating (0 to 60 points, lower means a harder transition) covering workload, confidence, belonging and support from preceptors. Right now the score is filed and nobody acts on it. Our nurse educators would like to use a cut-off, probably 30 or below, to offer a mentoring booster to residents who look likely to leave, but we do not know whether the score actually picks out the nurses who later go.

I would like to set up a diagnostic accuracy study of the month-3 Transition Check, with separation from the hospital within 12 months of hire as the reference standard, taken from human resources dates by someone who never sees the scores. Before we build the booster around the score we need the sensitivity and specificity at the proposed cut-off, how many residents we would flag, and how many of the flagged residents would actually leave. The score must never be used in performance reviews, and the residents need to trust that. We have no research funding beyond the residency budget, and the study should run within the normal residency schedule for the intakes starting in October 2026.
inputs.constraints: No research funding beyond the residency budget. The Transition Check is completed during the month-3 seminar and must add no extra resident time. Scores are never shared with nurse managers or used in performance reviews. Human resources can release hire and separation dates only, not exit reasons.

Human resources signed a data release memorandum on 2026-08-12 (HR-DR-2026-12) for hire and separation dates of consenting residents, prepared by an analyst who never sees Transition Check scores.
The four intakes from October 2026 to October 2027 are expected to total about 280 new graduates.
In the 2023 to 2025 intakes, 19 to 26 percent of residents separated from the hospital within 12 months of hire (residency office summary).

records.title: Accuracy of a month-3 transition self-rating for predicting first-year separation among new graduate nurses
records.authors: Adebayo-Lund K, Moreau-Singh T, Halvorsen-Oyelaran J
records.abstract: Background: early identification of new graduate nurses at risk of leaving could focus retention support. Methods: in two teaching hospitals, 412 residents completed a 15-item transition self-rating at month 3, and separation from the employing hospital within 12 months of hire was taken from human resources records by staff blind to the scores. Results: 79 residents (19 percent) separated. At a score of 30 or below, sensitivity was 0.71 (95 percent CI 0.60 to 0.81) and specificity 0.68 (0.63 to 0.73); the area under the ROC curve was 0.74. Positive predictive value was 0.35 at the observed prevalence. Conclusions: the self-rating identified most nurses who later left but flagged many who stayed, and the threshold should be validated locally before use.

records.title: Transition shock in the first year of practice: validation of a 15-item self-rating scale for new graduate nurses
records.abstract: We examined the measurement properties of a 15-item self-rating of transition difficulty completed by 638 new graduate nurses in five hospitals. Items cover workload, clinical confidence, belonging and preceptor support, scored 0 to 4 and summed to 0 to 60. Internal consistency was high (Cronbach alpha 0.88) and a four-factor structure fitted the data acceptably. Test-retest reliability over two weeks was 0.81 in a subsample of 94 nurses. Scores were lowest between months 3 and 4 of practice and rose thereafter. The scale was not evaluated against later turnover, and the authors caution that it measures experienced difficulty rather than intention to leave.

records.title: Nurse residency programmes and first-year retention of new graduate nurses: a systematic review
records.authors: Castillo-Hartmann R, Nwachukwu-Berg L, Fairweather-Iqbal S
records.abstract: We searched four bibliographic databases to 2020 for studies reporting 12-month retention of new graduate nurses with and without a structured residency programme. Twenty-four studies met the criteria, 21 of them before-after comparisons within single organisations. Reported 12-month retention ranged from 78 to 94 percent with a residency and from 64 to 88 percent without. Programme content, length and the definition of retention varied widely, and nine studies counted internal transfers as losses. No included study evaluated a screening step to target extra support. Certainty was low because of uncontrolled designs and inconsistent outcome definitions.

records.title: Stated intention to leave and actual separation among early-career nurses: a 12-month follow-up
records.abstract: Intention to leave is often used as a stand-in for turnover. We asked 355 nurses in their first two years of practice at six months whether they intended to leave their employer within a year, and followed actual separation in human resources records. Sixty-two nurses (17 percent) separated. Stated intention identified 30 of them (sensitivity 0.48) and was absent in 253 of the 293 who stayed (specificity 0.86). Nurses who left for family or relocation reasons rarely reported an intention in advance. The authors conclude that stated intention misses about half of later leavers and should not be the only trigger for retention support.

records.title: Human resources records as the reference standard for nurse turnover research: completeness and misclassification of separation data
records.authors: Whitcombe-Adeyemi F, Tanaka-Riordan P, Bello-Sorensen C
records.abstract: We compared human resources separation records for 1,904 nurses in three hospitals with payroll end dates and manager confirmation. Separation dates were present and correct for 99 percent of nurses who left. Reason codes were less reliable: 23 percent of separations coded as resignations were internal transfers to another unit or site of the same organisation, and 9 percent of retirements were coded as resignations. The authors recommend defining turnover as leaving the organisation, using dates rather than reason codes, and stating before analysis how internal transfers are handled.

records.title: A targeted mentoring booster for new graduate nurses with low transition scores: a before-after evaluation
records.abstract: One hospital offered six additional mentoring sessions to new graduate nurses who scored in the lowest quarter of a transition self-rating at month 3. Twelve-month retention of all residents was 81 percent in the two years before the booster and 88 percent in the two years after. Uptake among eligible residents was 64 percent. Other changes during the period included a new preceptor allowance and a regional hiring freeze, and the evaluation had no concurrent comparison group. The authors suggest that a screening threshold should be validated before a booster is tied to it.

records.title: Prevalence of first-year separation and the stability of screening thresholds across hospitals
records.authors: Iwu-Castellano B, Ferreira-Nakamura O, Holm-Achterberg V
records.abstract: Using transition ratings and human resources data from 11 hospitals, we examined how the usefulness of a fixed screening threshold changed with local separation rates. First-year separation ranged from 12 to 27 percent between hospitals. Sensitivity and specificity at a fixed threshold varied little, but the positive predictive value ranged from 0.21 at 12 percent separation to 0.44 at 27 percent. Two hospitals whose residency seminars were held later in the first year showed lower sensitivity. The authors recommend reporting predictive values at the local prevalence and fixing the timing of the rating.

response.synthesis: Seven retrieved records, appraised at abstract level. One two-hospital study reports that a month-3 transition self-rating at 30 or below had sensitivity 0.71 and specificity 0.68 for separation within 12 months, with a positive predictive value of 0.35; a multi-hospital analysis shows predictive values shift with the local separation rate. The scale itself is reliable, human resources dates are an accurate reference standard when internal transfers are handled explicitly, and stated intention to leave misses about half of leavers. A booster tied to a low score was followed by better retention only in an uncontrolled comparison. The evidence supports measuring the accuracy of the cut-off locally before acting on it.
response.gradeRationale: One accuracy study with the threshold chosen in its own data, supported by measurement and reference-standard studies; imprecise and indirect for this hospital's separation rate. Certainty that the cut-off performs as reported here is low.
response.summary: Seven retrieved records appraised; four source-derived claims recorded with passages; overall certainty low.

response.reading: The Transition Check is collected at the point where transition difficulty peaks, but nobody links it to the outcome that matters to the hospital. Retrieved evidence suggests the score separates future leavers from stayers only moderately, and that what a positive result means depends on the local separation rate. The reference standard is available and accurate by date, provided internal transfers are counted as staying. The main human risk is that a flag becomes a label: managers must never see scores, and residents must trust that the check is for support.

response.sampleSize: About 280 residents are expected across four intakes. At 20 percent separation, about 56 residents will separate and 224 will stay. With an expected sensitivity of 0.70, 56 separations give a 95 percent confidence interval of about plus or minus 0.12 (1.96 x sqrt(0.70 x 0.30 / 56)); an expected specificity of 0.68 with 224 stayers gives about plus or minus 0.06. A half-width of 0.10 for sensitivity would need about 81 separations, roughly six intakes; the team accepts plus or minus 0.12 for a local decision about the booster and will report the intervals as they are.

response.risks: Minimal physical risk. The main risks are that a low score becomes a label, that managers learn individual scores, and that residents feel surveilled; scores never leave the residency office and are not used for performance or employment decisions.
response.consent: Verbal consent at the month-3 seminar after a short information sheet that states who sees the score, what human resources shares, and that declining changes nothing about the residency; consent can be withdrawn until the 12-month extract.
response.data: Study numbers link scores and dates; the name key is held only by the residency office; the analysis file holds no names, no unit and no manager; files are kept on the hospital research drive and destroyed five years after publication.
response.equity: PROGRESS-Plus: residents who are first in their family to attend university, internationally raised graduates, residents with caring responsibilities and those on night-heavy rotations or at the rural campus may experience transition differently. Accuracy is reported descriptively for these groups, and the booster, if built, is offered on request to anyone regardless of score.
response.effectiveness: The study succeeds if it gives a local estimate precise enough to decide whether the cut-off can target the booster; a poor result is a useful answer that points to offering support to everyone.
response.efficiency: Uses a check already completed and dates already held; about one hour of analyst time per intake.
response.costs: Residency coordinator and analyst time within existing roles; no participant payments.
response.grants: None needed; a positive result could support a nursing education grant to evaluate the booster itself.
response.partnerships: Residency educators, the human resources analytics team, two residents from the previous intake as advisors, and the nurses' union representative for the information sheet.
response.rebPath: Approved by the hospital research ethics board on 2026-07-30 (REB-2026-417) with verbal consent; the human resources release is covered by HR-DR-2026-12.
response.limitations: Single hospital; early leavers are not tested; the estimate is imprecise with about 56 separations.
response.summary: Minimal-risk accuracy study with verbal consent, scores withheld from managers, and descriptive equity reporting.

response.partnershipPlan: Two residents from the June 2026 intake review the information sheet and the month-6 item before October; a preceptor and the union representative join the planning meeting; the human resources analyst confirms the extract steps.

response.title: Accuracy of a month-3 transition self-rating for identifying new graduate nurses who leave within 12 months of hire: a single-site diagnostic accuracy study
response.abstract: Objective: to estimate the sensitivity and specificity of a month-3 Transition Check score of 30 or below for separation from the hospital within 12 months of hire. Design: diagnostic accuracy study in four residency intakes, October 2026 to October 2027. Reference standard: separation date in human resources records, ascertained blind to the score. Results and conclusions will be written after the last reference-standard extract.
response.introduction: One in five new graduate nurses leaves the hospital within a year of hire. A month-3 self-rating is already collected, and one external study suggests it identifies most later leavers while flagging many who stay. The hospital needs a local estimate before it ties a mentoring booster to the score.
response.methods: All residents attending the month-3 seminar are eligible. The cut-off of 30 or below was fixed in advance. Separation dates are released by a human resources analyst who does not see the scores, and transfers between units count as staying. Sensitivity and specificity are reported with Wilson intervals and predictive values at the local separation rate.
response.results: No data have been collected yet. The report will present the STARD flow diagram, the 2 by 2 table, sensitivity and specificity with intervals, the ROC curve and predictive values.
response.discussion: The discussion will compare local accuracy with the external estimate, weigh how many flagged residents would stay anyway, and state whether the cut-off can target the booster.
response.limitations: Single site; residents who leave before month 3 are untested; about 56 separations limit precision.
response.conclusion: To be written after the analysis; it will be limited to the accuracy of this cut-off in this hospital.

store.title: Month-3 Transition Check and separation of new graduate nurses within 12 months of hire
store.problem.rawNeed:
I coordinate the 12-month nurse residency program for new graduate registered nurses at our 640-bed regional teaching hospital. We take three intakes a year (February, June and October) of about 70 new graduates each. Retention is our biggest worry: in the last three years between 19 and 26 percent of each intake left the hospital within 12 months of hire, and every nurse who leaves costs us months of orientation and preceptor time.

At the month-3 residency seminar every resident completes our Transition Check, a 15-item self-rating (0 to 60 points, lower means a harder transition) covering workload, confidence, belonging and support from preceptors. Right now the score is filed and nobody acts on it. Our nurse educators would like to use a cut-off, probably 30 or below, to offer a mentoring booster to residents who look likely to leave, but we do not know whether the score actually picks out the nurses who later go.

I would like to set up a diagnostic accuracy study of the month-3 Transition Check, with separation from the hospital within 12 months of hire as the reference standard, taken from human resources dates by someone who never sees the scores. Before we build the booster around the score we need the sensitivity and specificity at the proposed cut-off, how many residents we would flag, and how many of the flagged residents would actually leave. The score must never be used in performance reviews, and the residents need to trust that. We have no research funding beyond the residency budget, and the study should run within the normal residency schedule for the intakes starting in October 2026.
